title: The AI stadium · AI in the Premier League

slides.name: 1 · Teacher page

params.text:
Students map where AI works across a whole football club on matchday, and decide where people must keep control.
Ten minutes. No phones, no join code: hands up, four corners and pair talk.
Every reveal is one click. Ask first, then press →.

slides.notes:
Themes from Youth Charter’s education packs. Our own copy, not their materials.

RUNNING ORDER · ABOUT 40 MINUTES (slide numbers are the shown slides)
· Cover — up as they come in
· The 95th minute — 1 min
· Four corners — 2 min, where does AI work hardest?
· What is AI? — 2 min
· How AI learns, and what AI can do — 2 min
· THE AI STADIUM — 1 min, the map and its twelve zones
· Zones 1–6, a slide each — 6 min
· Pair talk — 2 min, the sensor that knows you are tired
· Zones 7–12, a slide each — 5 min
· One league, one cloud — 2 min
· The numbers — 1 min
· The Klopp hire — 1 min
· Integrated intelligence — 2 min
· The 90/10 debate — 2 min
· Stand on the line — 3 min
· Myth or fact — 2 min
· Bad at team sports — 1 min
· Careers four corners — 2 min
· Three rules — 1 min
· Your move — 1 min
· The last word

FOR 30 MINUTES. Hide the 90/10 debate, stand on the line and myth or fact; keep a zone to 40 seconds.

THE BIG IDEA. Integrated intelligence: the clubs that win combine AI and data with human skills, like Jürgen Klopp’s people skills at Liverpool. Every zone on the map is AI plus a person, never AI alone. The Klopp hire and integrated intelligence say it out loud, and the 90/10 debate argues with it.

THE MAP. The map slide shows all twelve zones. Each of the next twelve slides is one zone: the map zooms in as it opens, and the panel says what happens there, which kinds of AI do it (the dark labels), how they work, who still decides and the catch. Read the yellow question and take two answers. Hover a zone to name it.

THE BASICS. "What is AI?" and "The kinds of AI" come before the map, so every zone can be named: machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, language AI, generative AI, simulation.

THE MOVE THAT MAKES IT WORK. Every zone has a catch. Do not sell the technology; let them argue about it.

SOURCES. The Premier League facts are from AI Awareness Day’s timeline post, “Did you know the English Premier League uses AI?”. Liverpool’s neuroscience work and the Klopp hire are from Ulrich Lichtenthaler, “Liverpool FC: Extending data analytics and AI with neuroscience” (May 2022). The Premier League Companion and the fan figures are Microsoft’s (unlocked.microsoft.com/premier-league and its customer story); treat them as the company’s claims. Reading’s head of AI is from BBC Sport, “Reading hope AI can take them to the Premier League” (6 March 2026). PLAIER’s simulations, the Kane prediction and the 90/10 claim are from Sky Sports, “AI revolution in football: how PLAIER is helping Premier League clubs make better decisions” (6 February 2025): the company’s own findings. William Spearman’s words are from the Mirror (21 September 2022), quoting Liverpoolfc.com. The 1.3% goal probability and Moneyball are from Liverpool.com, “Liverpool are using incredible data science during matches” (15 January 2020). The negotiation clone is from OneFootball (10 June 2026), reporting the Telegraph: the software is Nostrada.ai, and clubs were said to be considering it, not yet using it. The other zones say what clubs and grounds can do, not what one named club does.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Give pairs a printed map and twelve sticky dots: they place a dot where they think AI is before slide 4.

EXTENSION. Design one new zone: where else in a club could AI help, and what would its catch be?

slides.name: 2 · The AI stadium
slides.notes: COVER. Up as the class comes in. Ask the door: "How many computers do you think are working at a Premier League match?"

slides.name: 3 · Ninety-five minutes on the clock. The ball hits the net. Before the celebration ends, the cameras have already found the foul.

params.text: Ninety-five minutes on the clock. The ball hits the net. Before the celebration ends, the cameras have already found the foul.

slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 1 MINUTE. From the AI Awareness Day post: West Ham scored what looked like a late equaliser against Arsenal; multiple camera angles were checked in seconds and the foul on goalkeeper David Raya was found. The 1-0 stood.

Ask: "Was that fair? Would you feel differently if you supported West Ham?"

slides.name: 4 · Where does AI work hardest on matchday?

params.text: Where does AI work hardest on matchday?

slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 2 MINUTES. Everyone moves. One reason from each corner.

The answer is all four, which the map shows next. Remember who stood where: come back to it after slide 6.

slides.name: 5 · Framed picture
slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 2 MINUTES. THE BASICS. Ask first: "What is AI?" Take two answers.

Then the picture, from the outside in. AI is the big idea: computers doing jobs that usually need human intelligence, like seeing, predicting or understanding language. Machine learning is one way to build it: instead of writing every rule, you show the computer lots of examples and it learns the pattern. Deep learning is machine learning with many layers of artificial “neurons”, which is what made computers good at pictures and speech. Generative AI is deep learning that makes something new: words, images, video.

Check: "Is a calculator AI?" (No: it follows fixed rules and learns nothing.) "Is a spam filter AI?" (Yes: it learned what spam looks like.)

slides.name: 6 · How AI learns and predicts

params.text: Learns patterns from past examples. In football: warns that a player is at risk of injury.
Learns from huge amounts of data, in many layers. In football: finds every player’s joints in a video.
Plays out “what if” thousands of times. In football: plays the season 10,000 times.

slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 1 MINUTE. The engines. Machine learning and deep learning are how AI learns; simulation uses what it learned to try thousands of futures.

Simulation on its own is not always AI, but in football it usually runs on what machine learning has learned.

slides.name: 7 · What AI can do

params.text: Sees and understands pictures and video. In football: draws the offside line.
Understands and writes human language. In football: writes scouting reports.
Makes new words, pictures or video. In football: answers fans in a chatbot.

slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 1 MINUTE. The jobs. NLP means natural language processing. Every zone on the map uses at least one of these six kinds: watch for the dark labels on each zone’s page.

Ask: "Which one have you used today?" Face unlock is computer vision; autocorrect and voice assistants are language AI; a chatbot is generative AI; a recommended video is machine learning.

figureData.source: Sources: AI Awareness Day · Microsoft · BBC · Sky Sports · OneFootball · Mirror · Liverpool.com · U. Lichtenthaler

cloud.name: One league, one cloud
cloud.does: Every zone sends its data to the same place: tickets, cameras, sensors, scouting, prices, your app.
cloud.how: The Premier League is building one media, data and AI platform with Microsoft, its official Cloud and AI partner, for 1.8 billion fans.
cloud.risk: Data collected to keep you safe can be used to sell to you.
cloud.ask: Who should be allowed to see all of it?

gates.name: Gates & turnstiles
gates.does: Tickets on phones are scanned at the turnstiles. Software counts fans in and predicts where queues will build, so stewards can open more gates early.
gates.how: Machine learning learns from past matchdays when crowds arrive. Computer vision can read faces, which some police forces have trialled outside grounds.
gates.decides: The stewards and the ground’s safety officer.
gates.risk: If your face becomes your ticket, your face is on a database.
gates.ask: Would you scan your face to get in quicker?

control.name: Safety control room
control.does: CCTV software watches stairways and concourses, and warns the safety team when a crowd gets too packed or starts moving the wrong way.
control.how: Computer vision counts people in each camera picture and spots crowding patterns faster than a person watching dozens of screens.
control.decides: The safety officer. Keeping 50,000 people safe is a human job.
control.risk: The cameras watch everyone, not only the trouble.
control.ask: Is being watched the price of being safe?

stands.name: The stands
stands.does: The club app holds your ticket, lets you order food to your seat, and suggests offers.
stands.how: Machine learning finds patterns in what fans like you bought before, and predicts what you will want next.
stands.risk: The app learns where you sit, what you buy and when you leave.
stands.ask: What does your phone tell the club about you?

pitch.name: The pitch & the officials
pitch.does: Semi-automated offside tracks dozens of points on every player’s body, and a chip in the ball. VAR checks camera angles in seconds.
pitch.how: Deep learning has been trained on thousands of hours of video to find players’ joints in every frame, so a computer can draw the offside line.
pitch.decides: The referee and the VAR officials. The machine draws the line; people make the call.
pitch.risk: Everyone waits for the check before they can celebrate.
pitch.ask: Would you trade the wait for a fairer result?

dugout.name: Dugout & analysts’ box
dugout.does: Analysts track every player 25 times a second to see which team controls which space, and test thousands of corner routines before a match.
dugout.how: Machine learning turns tracking into “pitch control”. Google DeepMind’s TacticAI, a deep learning model, suggests where players should stand at corners.
dugout.decides: The manager picks the team and the tactics.
dugout.risk: If every club follows the same models, football gets more predictable.
dugout.ask: Should a manager ever ignore what the data says?

medical.name: Dressing room & medical
medical.does: GPS vests and sensors measure every sprint and heartbeat, in training and in matches.
medical.how: Machine learning compares a player’s numbers with thousands of past injuries, and flags when tired muscles are at risk of a tear.
medical.decides: The medical team and the player.
medical.risk: A player’s body becomes data. Who owns it?
medical.ask: Would you wear a sensor that tells your coach you are tired?

tv.name: TV gantry & media
tv.does: Highlights are cut in seconds, and live graphics show each team’s chance of winning.
tv.how: Computer vision spots goals, shots and celebrations in the video. The Opta supercomputer simulates the season 10,000 times to get the chances.
tv.decides: The TV director chooses what millions of people see.
tv.risk: The highlights pick which players become famous.

grounds.name: Pitch care & energy
grounds.does: Sensors under the grass measure moisture and temperature, and help decide when to water, light and mow.
grounds.how: Machine learning finds the pattern between weather, sensor readings and how the grass grows.
grounds.decides: The head groundsperson, who knows the pitch.
grounds.risk: A sensor can say the grass is fine when a player knows it is not.
grounds.ask: Where would you trust the sensor over the expert?

training.name: Training ground & academy
training.does: Every session is filmed and tracked. Liverpool also worked with neuro11, a neuroscience company, to train players’ focus for penalties.
training.how: Computer vision tracks the players on film; machine learning plans how hard each one should work this week. Academies collect the same data on young players.
training.risk: Data on a 12-year-old can label them too early.
training.ask: Should data decide who gets released from an academy?

scouting.name: Scouting office
scouting.does: Clubs search for players across the world. Reading made the first head of AI at an English club to find players they never knew about.
scouting.how: PLAIER’s machine learning rates players from data on over 100 leagues, simulates a signing’s season 100,000 times, and writes reports in plain words.
scouting.decides: The scouts. Reading kept its human scouts; the AI gives them more players to look at.
scouting.risk: A player in a league with no data is invisible to the machine.
scouting.ask: Who gets missed when scouting runs on data?

business.name: Club business
business.does: Clubs use data to set prices and sell sponsorship. At least three Premier League clubs are reported to be exploring an AI copy of rival clubs, to practise transfer deals.
business.how: Machine learning predicts demand for each match. The copy is a generative AI chatbot built on data about clubs’ past transfers.
business.risk: The copy is built from what real people said and did. Nobody asked them.
business.ask: Is it fair to practise a deal against an AI copy of the other side?

home.name: Fans at home
home.does: The Premier League Companion, built with Microsoft, answers fans’ questions from 30 seasons of stats and live data. The Fantasy Premier League Companion helps pick your team.
home.how: A generative AI chatbot reads your question in your own language and writes an answer from the league’s data. Language AI also filters abuse aimed at players.
home.decides: You pick your team. Platforms decide what you are shown.
home.risk: It learns what keeps you on the app, and abuse still gets past filters.
home.ask: Is it still your team if an AI picked it?

cloud.name: One league, one cloud
cloud.does: Every zone sends its data to the same place: tickets, cameras, sensors, scouting, prices, your app.

gates.name: Gates & turnstiles
gates.does: Tickets on phones are scanned at the turnstiles. Software counts fans in and predicts where queues will build, so stewards can open more gates early.
gates.how: Machine learning learns from past matchdays when crowds arrive. Computer vision can read faces, which some police forces have trialled outside grounds.
gates.decides: The stewards and the ground’s safety officer.
gates.risk: If your face becomes your ticket, your face is on a database.
gates.ask: Would you scan your face to get in quicker?

control.name: Safety control room
control.does: CCTV software watches stairways and concourses, and warns the safety team when a crowd gets too packed or starts moving the wrong way.
control.how: Computer vision counts people in each camera picture and spots crowding patterns faster than a person watching dozens of screens.
control.decides: The safety officer. Keeping 50,000 people safe is a human job.
control.risk: The cameras watch everyone, not only the trouble.
control.ask: Is being watched the price of being safe?

stands.name: The stands
stands.does: The club app holds your ticket, lets you order food to your seat, and suggests offers.
stands.how: Machine learning finds patterns in what fans like you bought before, and predicts what you will want next.
stands.risk: The app learns where you sit, what you buy and when you leave.
stands.ask: What does your phone tell the club about you?

pitch.name: The pitch & the officials
pitch.does: Semi-automated offside tracks dozens of points on every player’s body, and a chip in the ball. VAR checks camera angles in seconds.
pitch.how: Deep learning has been trained on thousands of hours of video to find players’ joints in every frame, so a computer can draw the offside line.
pitch.decides: The referee and the VAR officials. The machine draws the line; people make the call.
pitch.risk: Everyone waits for the check before they can celebrate.
pitch.ask: Would you trade the wait for a fairer result?

dugout.name: Dugout & analysts’ box
dugout.does: Analysts track every player 25 times a second to see which team controls which space, and test thousands of corner routines before a match.
dugout.how: Machine learning turns tracking into “pitch control”. Google DeepMind’s TacticAI, a deep learning model, suggests where players should stand at corners.
dugout.decides: The manager picks the team and the tactics.
dugout.risk: If every club follows the same models, football gets more predictable.
dugout.ask: Should a manager ever ignore what the data says?

medical.name: Dressing room & medical
medical.does: GPS vests and sensors measure every sprint and heartbeat, in training and in matches.
medical.how: Machine learning compares a player’s numbers with thousands of past injuries, and flags when tired muscles are at risk of a tear.
medical.decides: The medical team and the player.
medical.risk: A player’s body becomes data. Who owns it?
medical.ask: Would you wear a sensor that tells your coach you are tired?

tv.name: TV gantry & media
tv.does: Highlights are cut in seconds, and live graphics show each team’s chance of winning.
tv.how: Computer vision spots goals, shots and celebrations in the video. The Opta supercomputer simulates the season 10,000 times to get the chances.
tv.decides: The TV director chooses what millions of people see.
tv.risk: The highlights pick which players become famous.

grounds.name: Pitch care & energy
grounds.does: Sensors under the grass measure moisture and temperature, and help decide when to water, light and mow.
grounds.how: Machine learning finds the pattern between weather, sensor readings and how the grass grows.
grounds.decides: The head groundsperson, who knows the pitch.
grounds.risk: A sensor can say the grass is fine when a player knows it is not.
grounds.ask: Where would you trust the sensor over the expert?

training.name: Training ground & academy
training.does: Every session is filmed and tracked. Liverpool also worked with neuro11, a neuroscience company, to train players’ focus for penalties.
training.how: Computer vision tracks the players on film; machine learning plans how hard each one should work this week. Academies collect the same data on young players.
training.risk: Data on a 12-year-old can label them too early.
training.ask: Should data decide who gets released from an academy?

scouting.name: Scouting office
scouting.does: Clubs search for players across the world. Reading made the first head of AI at an English club to find players they never knew about.
scouting.how: PLAIER’s machine learning rates players from data on over 100 leagues, simulates a signing’s season 100,000 times, and writes reports in plain words.
scouting.decides: The scouts. Reading kept its human scouts; the AI gives them more players to look at.
scouting.risk: A player in a league with no data is invisible to the machine.
scouting.ask: Who gets missed when scouting runs on data?

business.name: Club business
business.does: Clubs use data to set prices and sell sponsorship. At least three Premier League clubs are reported to be exploring an AI copy of rival clubs, to practise transfer deals.
business.how: Machine learning predicts demand for each match. The copy is a generative AI chatbot built on data about clubs’ past transfers.
business.risk: The copy is built from what real people said and did. Nobody asked them.
business.ask: Is it fair to practise a deal against an AI copy of the other side?

home.name: Fans at home
home.does: The Premier League Companion, built with Microsoft, answers fans’ questions from 30 seasons of stats and live data. The Fantasy Premier League Companion helps pick your team.
home.how: A generative AI chatbot reads your question in your own language and writes an answer from the league’s data. Language AI also filters abuse aimed at players.
home.decides: You pick your team. Platforms decide what you are shown.
home.risk: It learns what keeps you on the app, and abuse still gets past filters.
home.ask: Is it still your team if an AI picked it?

slides.name: 23 · The numbers behind matchday

params.text: Chance of a goal in the next 15 seconds — Liverpool’s model, from where the ball and players are
Premier League fans, in 189 countries — Microsoft and the Premier League’s figure
Penalties Liverpool scored in a cup final shootout — after neuroscience training, February 2022

params.label: Takeaway
params.text: Sources: Liverpool.com (2020) on pitch control; Microsoft, “AI at the heart of the beautiful game” (2026); Ulrich Lichtenthaler (2022) on Liverpool and neuro11

slides.notes:
BEAT 21 · 1 MINUTE. Liverpool’s Director of Research, William Spearman, has a PhD in particle physics and worked at CERN. Ask: "Did you think football clubs hired physicists?"

The 1.3%: Liverpool’s data scientist Tim Waskett, an astrophysicist, showed at the Royal Institution Christmas Lectures how the club turns every moment of a match into a goal probability: with the ball in one position, a 1.3% chance of a goal in the next 15 seconds (Liverpool.com, January 2020). Every pass changes the number. Ask: "Which pass would you make to push it up?"

The 1.8 billion: Microsoft says the Premier League Companion reached 60 million active fans in its first two months, with 20% more engagement on the league’s app and website. Those are Microsoft’s own figures, from its customer story; say so.

The 11 of 11: Liverpool beat Chelsea on penalties in the February 2022 League Cup final, with every Liverpool taker scoring. Jürgen Klopp credited neuro11, a German neuroscience company the club had worked with since 2021, for preparing players for penalties and set pieces.

slides.name: 24 · Why Liverpool hired Jürgen Klopp

params.text: Klopp’s last season at Borussia Dortmund went badly, and the papers criticised him.
Liverpool’s research team, led by Ian Graham, found Dortmund had been very unlucky. Klopp was still one of the best.
Liverpool hired him. They won the Champions League in 2019 and the Premier League in 2020.

slides.notes:
BEAT 22 · 1 MINUTE. From Ulrich Lichtenthaler (2022): after a bad final season at Borussia Dortmund, Klopp was heavily criticised. Liverpool’s Head of Research, Ian Graham, and his team showed that Dortmund had been very unlucky and that Klopp was still one of the best managers. Liverpool won the Champions League in 2019 and the Premier League in 2020.

Ask: "So did the data win those trophies?" Take answers, then the next slide.

slides.name: 25 · Integrated intelligence

params.text: Tracks every player 25 times a second.
Spots who is having a bad week at home.
Picks the moment to take a risk.
Finds players in data from around the world.
Sees who will fit the dressing room.
Trains players’ focus for the shootout.
Puts an arm round the one who missed.

slides.notes:
BEAT 23 · 2 MINUTES. THE BIG IDEA. Lichtenthaler calls it integrated intelligence: Liverpool’s data and AI only paid off when they were combined with Klopp’s emotional intelligence and people skills. Neither side wins alone.

Read each AI line, ask "and what does a person bring?", take an answer, then click. Then: "Go back to the map. Which zone has AI with no person beside it?" (None should.)

Liverpool.com (2020) put it simply: whatever the data scientists find, Klopp has to interpret it and apply it in a footballing sense. Liverpool’s owners have trusted data for a long time: John Henry once offered Billy Beane, the man behind Moneyball, the job of running the Boston Red Sox.

The same idea from BBC Sport (March 2026): Professor Nick Jennings of Loughborough University says AI “complements human expertise and human insight”, and Reading’s head of AI says that for now it complements the team, and results are down to the coaches.

slides.name: 26 · Statement · frame

params.text: An AI company says players are 90% of a team’s success, and the coach only 10%.
Agree or disagree · hands up · 2 minutes

slides.notes:
BEAT 24 · 2 MINUTES. THE DEBATE. Hands up: agree, disagree, not sure. Then one reason from each side.

From Sky Sports (February 2025): Jan Wendt, co-founder of PLAIER, said its models found player quality responsible for around 90% of success and the coach around 10%, though 10% can still make the difference. PLAIER also said Klopp’s Liverpool performed about as well as its squad should have.

Set that against the last two slides: Lichtenthaler credits Klopp’s people skills. Who is right? Maybe both: the coach is part of why the players got that good. That is integrated intelligence again.

params.text: Who you are, from your face
The positions are arguable. That is the activity.

slides.notes:
BEAT 25 · 3 MINUTES. STAND ON THE LINE. One wall "AI can decide", the opposite wall "a person must decide". Read each item, students move, then click to show where we put it.

Ask: "Which one did we put in the wrong place?" The academy is the one to land.

slides.name: 28 · Myth or fact?

params.text: AI picks the Premier League teams
Managers pick the team. AI gives them evidence.
The supercomputer knows who will win
It gives chances, not answers. Upsets still happen.
Liverpool’s research team includes physicists and an astrophysicist.
Signing a superstar always makes a team better
An AI model predicted Harry Kane would not improve Bayern. Their goal difference fell.

slides.notes:
Row 4 is from Sky Sports (February 2025): PLAIER’s model predicted Bayern’s record signing would not have a positive effect, and Bayern’s goal difference was 49 with him against 54 the season before (PLAIER’s figures). It is no slight on Kane: football is a team game.

BEAT 26 · 2 MINUTES. Thumbs up for true, down for false, then click for the fact.

Row 3 is a good one to argue: if the computer says 70%, who is surprised when the 30% happens?

slides.name: 29 · I grew up being really bad at most team sports. I still am.

params.text: I grew up being really bad at most team sports. I still am.
— William Spearman, lead data scientist, Liverpool

slides.notes:
BEAT 27 · 1 MINUTE. You do not have to be good at football to work in football. Spearman did a physics PhD, got hooked on sports data watching American football, and now works in Liverpool’s six-person research team on transfers and tactics. His best-known idea is “pitch control”: which areas of the pitch a team controls, so that a pass there would reach them, and how runs create and close space.

Source: the Mirror (21 September 2022), quoting his interview with Liverpoolfc.com.

Ask: "What are you really good at that is not football?"

slides.name: 30 · Which job would you want?

params.text: Builds the models that flag injuries.
Breaks down every match, frame by frame.
Reading made the first one at an English club.

slides.notes:
BEAT 28 · 2 MINUTES. From the AI Awareness Day post: "The sports industry is hungry for tech talent."

Everyone picks a corner. Ask: "What do you already do that is a start? Gaming, maths, coding, stats, editing videos?" Link to Youth Charter’s digital tech pathway.

Head of AI is a real job title now: BBC Sport (March 2026) reported that Reading, in League One, appointed Stuart Fenton as the first head of AI at an English club, working on recruitment, tactics and the business. Reading point to Brentford and Brighton as clubs that climbed using data.

params.text: Three rules for the AI stadium
In the order you would use them
Tickets, faces, bodies, clicks: know what is being measured.
Keep people in the big calls
AI can measure. People decide what is fair.
You can ask a club or app what it holds about you.

slides.notes:
BEAT 29 · 1 MINUTE. One rule per click.

Rule 3 is real: under UK data protection law anyone can ask an organisation for the personal data it holds about them.
